newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sees benefits from new tax code.
newsitem.headline: Russia sees benefits from new tax code.

text.p: Russia's new tax code will bring major economic benefits even though it could cost the government money, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Thursday.

Deputy Finance Minister Sergei Shatalov told a news conference after the weekly cabinet meeting that the government hoped the new tax code, now being drawn up by the government and going through parliament, would come into force next year.
"We must start 1998 with the new tax code," Shatalov said.
The new code will simplify the unwieldy and contradictory Russian tax system, meeting a long-standing demand of foreign investors and local businesses.
If the new tax code had been applied this year, the government would have lost 20 trillion roubles of the 315.71 trillion planned in the 1997 budget, Shatalov said.
But economic conditions in 1998 would differ from 1997 with a lower inflation rate and higher industrial output, he said.
Even if this does not happen, the new code is a necessary stage in restructuring the economy, he said.
"If this does not happen, we shall have to cut our expenditure," he said.
"Russia does not only face the problem of collecting taxes. We have to carry out economic reform and the new tax code is now the major step. The game is worth the candle."
The code will cut the share of tax in gross domestic product by 1.1 percentage points from the current 36 percent, he said.
It will cut the number of taxes, including sales tax, cancel most tax privileges, shift the tax burden to individuals from companies and simplify and clarify the whole tax system.
The first part of the code is to be debated by the State Duma lower house of parliament next month, and the government intends to finish work on the remaining three sections in a month, he said.
Foreign investors in Russia have long complained that the tax system is unpredictable and unstable.
Legislation changes often and is frequently unclear so that companies often do not know what their full tax liability is, encouraging many simply not to pay.
A 1992 decree allowed regional authorities to levy their own taxes or raise tax rates imposed by the federal government.
The decree led to the appearance of over 150 different taxes, including a levy on driving cattle.

The new tax code will provide a full list of taxes and their rates -- about 30 -- that can be levied. Regional authorities will no longer have the right to levy taxes not approved by the federal authorities or raise tax rates.
